> 大成若缺，其用不敝。大盈若沖，其用不窮.

Chapter 41 gave eleven 如's, all of them "looks wrong." Chapter 45 goes one layer deeper: it is not only that the real thing looks unlike itself — it deliberately keeps one place unclosed.

Five 大's, five 若's: 大成, 大盈, 大直, 大巧, 大辯. Each leaves exactly one thing unfinished: 缺, 沖, 屈, 拙, 訥.

And the two key characters in the chapter are both words for breakage.

## 缺 and 敝

缺: 器破也 — a vessel with a broken rim. 敝: worn-out cloth, a garment that has frayed.

So: 大成若缺，其用不敝. The great completion looks like a broken vessel, and its use does not wear out.

Turn it around and the sentence says: the thing that does not break is the one that already has a break in it.

That is not a paradox for charm. It is the same mechanism as chapter 22's 曲則全. A form with no gap is a form under continuous stress: every force has to be absorbed at the surface, and the surface has nowhere to yield.

A form with one open place has somewhere to give. The crack is where the strain goes.

## 大盈若沖

Great fullness looks like emptiness. 沖 is the surge, the flowing-through — the same character as 沖氣以為和 in chapter 42.

The fullness is inside; the emptiness is outside. What is full and closed has to defend its contents; what is full and open keeps circulating, so 其用不窮 — its use is never exhausted.

## 大直若屈，大巧若拙，大辯若訥

Straight looks bent; skill looks clumsy; eloquence looks halting.

These three are the same principle applied to conduct rather than to objects.

大直若屈 — the truly straight does not need to prove its straightness. A line that announces its straightness needs a reference to be measured against, and measuring is a form of bending.

大巧若拙 — skill that looks like clumsiness. The surface of real skill is unimpressive: no display, because the display would be an extra operation, and extra operations cost accuracy.

大辯若訥 — the great argument looks tongue-tied. 訥 is slow speech, the mouth that will not move smoothly. The person who says exactly what can be held to does not speak fluently.

## 躁勝寒，靜勝熱

Agitation overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat.

This line looks like it wandered in from a different chapter, and it is the hinge. Both are real: move and you warm up; be still and heat becomes bearable.

Note that neither is a universal remedy. The chapter is not saying stillness is better than motion. It is saying each condition has its counter, and the counter is not the opposite of the condition — it is the state that can hold it.

## 清靜為天下正

Clarity and stillness are the 正 of the world.

正 is the standard, the upright — the same character as 以正治國 in chapter 57. Not "the world would be peaceful if everyone were calm," but: the measure by which anything is aligned.

## The shape of the five

Each 大 keeps one place unclosed, and each unclosed place is functional, not decorative.

Take one thing you have finished and ask where its 缺 is. If there is none — if every edge is sealed — that is usually where the maintenance cost lives.
